title: Close a casement window whose crank arm's shoe has dropped out of the sash track
instruction: The crank on this window turns but no longer moves the window. Get the crank working again and leave the window cranked shut.
context: Crank-out casement windows are common in North American homes. On a straight-arm operator, the arm's nylon shoe runs in a channel under the sash. If the arm is pushed down where the channel has its centre notch, the shoe drops out. After that the crank swings the arm freely and the sash just hangs on its hinges. Pushing the sash shut by hand closes the window but leaves the crank disconnected, so it won't open next time. The fix is to bring the notch over the shoe by setting the sash angle and the crank angle, push the shoe up into the channel, and then crank the window shut. I have no source for the share of homes with casements, so the context should not give a number.
real_product:
Andersen 400 Series (Perma-Shield) casement, size CR12. Unit is 17 in x 28-7/8 in (43.2 x 73.3 cm), from retailer and manual size listings. Visible glass is 12-5/8 in wide, from Andersen parts listings.

- Operator: Andersen straight-arm operator 1361312, from parts.andersenwindows.com. Arm 8-3/8 in (213 mm). It comes with a nylon shoe, cover and channel, and fits units made 1966/1981 to 1995.
- Track: universal straight-arm track 9052562, 15-1/2 in (394 mm), for 400 Series units made 1995 to present, with 12 in and 14 in operators.
- How the arm connects: the Andersen help centre (Operator Types) says it is "an operator arm that slides along a channel located along the interior bottom of the window sash".
- The notch: allaboutdoors.com (Andersen casement operator replacement article, covering Andersen wood casements 1932-1989) says "There is a notch in the center of the track which allows easy removal and reconnection of the nylon shoe". Family Handyman (How to repair old windows) says "Open the window until the crank arm bushing is aligned with the guide track notch. Push down on the arm to pop the bushing out of the track." So the fault is real and the shoe leaves the track downward.

Caveats:
- WindowParts lists Andersen channel 1361204 as "no notch in center; shoe snaps onto track", so not every vintage has the notch.
- Andersen says 400 Series units from 1998 on mostly use split-arm operators on a sash bracket, with no track.
- The ranker's 'Truth Encore-type' is wrong
fault:
The arm's nylon shoe has dropped out of the sash channel through the centre notch. Cranking swings the arm under the sash but does not move the sash, which sits free at about 30 degrees open.

The real product removes the claimed two-handed skill. The sash turns on a vertical hinge axis, so with the shoe out it has no gravity torque and stays where it is left. Nothing has to be held while the other hand works. The fix becomes a sequence one arm can do:
1. Set the sash.
2. Crank the shoe under the notch.
3. Lift the arm end about 3 to 5 mm so the shoe enters the channel.
4. Crank the window shut.

The 'ordinary way' that fails, cranking, fails visibly and harmlessly. Pushing the sash shut by hand is the easy way out, and only the scoring can block it.
skill:
The skill is lining up two angles: the sash angle carries the notch, and the crank angle carries the shoe, at the one place they meet. Then the shoe is pushed up into the channel in the 15 to 20 mm gap under the sash, and the window is cranked closed with the shoe held in the channel.

This is a peg-in-notch insertion plus cranking. Cranking alone is already covered (dexhand Grinder Crank, cited when #2216 was rejected; #1181 'already covered'). The insertion is a short, moderate-difficulty step.

If the operator pivot is on the hinge side, as Prime-Line's operator listing describes, the notch only meets the shoe at about 76 to 83 degrees open, near full open. That puts all the work beside the hinge jamb, within reach of one arm only.

reviewer_reasons:
wide-funnel deepen, 17 Nov: killed. Kill it. Reasons, most serious first:

1. The real product removes the forced two-handed skill. A vertical-hinge sash with the shoe out stays where it is left. Re-inserting the shoe is a one-arm sequence: set the sash, crank the shoe under the notch, lift the arm, crank shut. What is left is a peg-in-notch insertion plus cranking, and cranking is already covered.
2. Importance for Societal relatability is weak. Re-seating an operator shoe is an occasional repair on some casement vintages, not something most people do themselves. Andersen says most 400 Series units from 1998 on use split-arm operators with no track. Truth Encore/Maxim dual-arm operators keep the slider captive in its track, so the ranker's named product does not have the fault at all.
3. It is a second casement-window task beside accepted #2110, and a reattach-on-track recovery, a family with several final rejections.
4. Construct validity:
   - The pin hinge stands in for Andersen's 4-bar hinge.
   - Code drives the arm from the crank angle; the real gear ratio and turns from open to shut are unknown.
   - The arm's flex is modelled as a sprung pitch joint.
   - The nylon shoe sliding in a steel channel needs friction lowered from the kit default.
   - No primary drawing places the operator pivot. That decides whether alignment comes at about 35 or about 80 degrees.
5. Build:
   - A hinge-side operator puts the shoe at x 0.44, reachable only by the right arm with a tilted grip.
   - The fingers must straddle the arm in a 15 to 20 mm gap beside the sash.
   - Several crank turns on a horizontal-axis handle close to the robot base.
   - Contact physics for a shoe sliding in a channel is fragile at the kit's default friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic).
6. Scoring has to block pushing the sash shut by hand while the shoe stays loose; #751 was sent back three times for this same kind of bypass.

Given the blind test (strict reviewers give truly accepted tasks about 0.1 to 0.25 on paper), this concept is below that range. I made no task folder, claim or git change.
